title: Southeast Asia to deliver less than one-third of planned gas power capacity by 2030
gist: Wood Mackenzie forecasts only 14.9 GW of Southeast Asia's ~53 GW government-targeted gas-fired power pipeline will reach commercial operation by 2030, with just 11 GW of the pipeline having secured turbines and everything else facing five-year-plus lead times. The shortfall is concentrated in Vietnam (3.7 GW delivered against a 29.4 GW target) and comes as the region heads for net gas importer status by 2033 with LNG supplying over 80% of gas demand by 2050.

insights.claim: Across six major Southeast Asian power markets, governments target roughly 53 GW of new gas-fired capacity by 2030 but Wood Mackenzie forecasts only 14.9 GW will reach commercial operation.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A ~38 GW shortfall means regional gas and LNG demand forecasts anchored to government targets are materially too high through 2030.
insights.quote: governments are targeting approximately 53 GW of new gas-fired capacity by 2030. However, Wood Mackenzie forecasts that only 14.9 GW will reach commercial operation
insights.locator: Across six major Southeast Asian power markets

insights.claim: The binding constraint on Southeast Asian gas power is execution rather than planning, because new capacity depends on several critical enablers — LNG infrastructure, project financing and turbine availability — and a bottleneck in any one can delay an entire project.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Screen projects on the weakest enabler, not the announced target — single-point failure across three dependencies makes delivery probabilities multiplicative.
insights.quote: The challenge today is not planning power projects but executing them.
insights.locator: “The challenge today is not planning power projects

insights.claim: Volatile fuel cost, equipment shortages, financing constraints and infrastructure bottlenecks are jointly delaying Southeast Asian gas project development, widening the gap between government ambition and delivery.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Delay risk is systemic and correlated across the region, not idiosyncratic to any single country's permitting regime.
insights.locator: Southeast Asia is expected to deliver less than one-third

themes.theme: Turbine scarcity as the hard constraint

insights.claim: Only 11 GW of Southeast Asia's planned gas-to-power pipeline has secured gas turbines, and capacity without secured turbines faces delivery lead times of at least five years.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Turbine order books are the single best leading indicator of which announced projects are real; anything unordered today cannot commission before 2031.
insights.quote: only 11 GW of the planned gas-to-power pipeline has secured gas turbines. The remaining planned capacity, which has yet to secure gas turbines, is likely to face delivery lead times of at least five years.
insights.locator: The report, Is Southeast Asia Being Gaslighted?

insights.claim: Gas turbine shortages have emerged as the most visible constraint on Southeast Asian project timelines, ahead of fuel availability, LNG infrastructure, financing, permitting and equipment procurement.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Pricing power sits with turbine OEMs; the scarcity rent accrues upstream of the developers, not to them.
insights.locator: Energy security adds a new layer of complexity

insights.claim: Southeast Asian electricity demand is projected to grow 2.4-fold by 2050, outpacing China, Australia and South Korea.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Southeast Asia is the fastest-growing major power demand pool in Asia — the structural long for generation equipment, grid and fuel suppliers.
insights.quote: Southeast Asia's electricity demand is projected to grow 2.4-fold by 2050, outpacing China, Australia and South Korea.
insights.locator: Southeast Asia's electricity demand is projected

insights.claim: Southeast Asian power demand growth is being driven by industrial expansion, the China+1 manufacturing shift, and rising investment in semiconductor production, electronics and hyperscale data centres.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Power adequacy becomes a gating factor for the China+1 relocation thesis — supply-chain diversification runs into a generation shortfall.
insights.quote: Growth is being fuelled by industrial expansion, the China+1 manufacturing shift and rising investment in semiconductor production, electronics and hyperscale data centres.
insights.locator: Southeast Asia's electricity demand is projected

insights.claim: Gas demand from the Southeast Asian power sector will more than double between 2026 and 2050, accounting for more than one-quarter of regional electricity generation by mid-century.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The long-dated gas demand case survives the near-term delivery shortfall — the problem is timing, not terminal demand.
insights.locator: Wood Mackenzie forecasts that gas demand from the power sector

themes.theme: LNG import dependence and energy security

insights.claim: Southeast Asia is expected to become a net gas importer by 2033, with LNG supplying more than 80% of regional gas demand by 2050.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A structural new LNG import bloc emerges by the mid-2030s — relevant to long-dated LNG offtake, regas terminal and shipping demand.
insights.quote: Wood Mackenzie expects Southeast Asia to become a net gas importer by 2033, with LNG projected to supply more than 80% of regional gas demand by 2050.
insights.locator: Energy security adds a new layer of complexity

insights.claim: The long-held assumption that gas would enable Southeast Asia's energy transition by meeting demand, integrating renewables and maintaining energy security is now being challenged as delays mount and supply chains tighten.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: If gas cannot be delivered on schedule, policymakers substitute toward coal extension, solar or demand curtailment — watch for transition-pathway policy revisions.
insights.quote: As gas project delays mount and supply chains tighten, policymakers are being forced to rethink not only the role of gas in the near term, but also the long-term pathways to achieving their energy transition goals
insights.locator: “Gas was once seen as a key enabler

themes.theme: Vietnam and the Philippines: the shortfall extremes

insights.claim: Vietnam targets 29.4 GW of new gas-fired capacity by 2030 but Wood Mackenzie expects only 3.7 GW to come online, the region's widest ambition-to-delivery gap.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Roughly 26 GW of assumed Vietnamese gas capacity is unlikely to appear — a large downgrade to Vietnam-linked LNG import forecasts.
insights.quote: While the government targets 29.4 GW of new gas-fired capacity by 2030, Wood Mackenzie expects only 3.7 GW to come online.
insights.locator: Vietnam: the largest delivery gap

insights.claim: Vietnam's early LNG-to-power projects have exposed commercial challenges around fuel pricing and cost allocation, while uncertainty over domestic gas supply and project timing continues to delay development.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Vietnam's blocker is contractual — until pass-through of LNG cost to tariffs is resolved, new FIDs stay stalled regardless of turbine supply.
insights.locator: Vietnam: the largest delivery gap

insights.claim: The Philippines faces immediate supply adequacy problems, evidenced by simultaneous red alerts across the Luzon and Visayas grids in May 2026, and is forecast to deliver only 0.4 GW of new gas capacity against a roughly 2 GW target.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Philippine grid stress is already live, not prospective — expect scarcity pricing, emergency procurement and reliability-driven policy intervention.
insights.quote: highlighted by simultaneous red alerts across the Luzon and Visayas grids in May 2026
insights.locator: Philippines: delivery delays threaten reliability

insights.claim: Fragmented responsibility for long-term resource planning is a key structural challenge in the Philippines, distinct from project-level delays.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Institutional fragmentation means Philippine shortfalls persist even if turbines and financing free up — a slower fix than elsewhere.
insights.locator: Philippines: delivery delays threaten reliability

themes.theme: Country workarounds: Malaysia, Indonesia, Singapore, Thailand

insights.claim: Peninsular Malaysia is bridging near-term execution risk by extending nearly 5 GW of existing gas-fired capacity through 2030, and is forecast to add 5.9 GW of new capacity against a requirement of around 9.4 GW.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Life-extension of existing plant is the cheapest hedge against turbine scarcity — a template other markets are likely to copy, and a boost to O&M/service revenues.
insights.quote: Peninsular Malaysia is managing near-term execution risk by extending nearly 5 GW of existing gas-fired capacity through 2030
insights.locator: Malaysia: extending existing capacity

insights.claim: Malaysia's government is exploring the repurposing of retiring coal plants into renewable energy hubs.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Brownfield grid connections at retiring coal sites are a scarce, valuable asset for renewables developers in a constrained interconnection environment.
insights.locator: Malaysia: extending existing capacity

insights.claim: Indonesia has secured turbine supply for only 200 MW of its planned 8.4 GW gas pipeline, the lowest proportion of any Southeast Asian market analysed.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Effectively none of Indonesia's gas pipeline is deliverable this decade — treat Indonesian gas-power demand assumptions as near-zero to 2030.
insights.quote: Indonesia has secured turbine supply for only 200 MW of its planned 8.4 GW gas capacity pipeline, the lowest proportion among the markets analysed.
insights.locator: Indonesia: equipment constraints slow progress

insights.claim: Indonesia's abundant domestic coal reduces near-term reliability risk from gas delays but may also slow decarbonisation, pushing the country toward accelerated solar deployment alongside selective gas development.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Gas delays in Indonesia convert into coal persistence plus a solar acceleration — bearish Indonesian LNG import volumes, bullish Indonesian solar buildout.
insights.locator: Indonesia: equipment constraints slow progress

insights.claim: Singapore has secured turbine supply for all major projects expected before 2030, but its next procurement round for 1.8 GW of hydrogen-ready generation will test whether even well-prepared markets can navigate tightening global equipment supply.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Singapore's 1.8 GW hydrogen-ready tender is a clean read on global turbine market tightness — a failed or delayed round signals worse for everyone else.
insights.quote: its next procurement round for 1.8 GW of hydrogen-ready generation capacity will test whether even well-prepared markets can continue to navigate tightening global equipment supply
insights.locator: Singapore: best positioned, but not immune

insights.claim: Thailand's problem is oversupply rather than shortfall: draft PDP2024 targets 1.4 GW of new gas capacity by 2030 against a Wood Mackenzie forecast of 0.5 GW, while surplus generation is locked into long-term power purchase agreements.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Thailand is the outlier where capacity underdelivery is benign; the investable question there is PPA restructuring risk, not new build.
insights.quote: Thailand's challenge is managing an oversupplied power system.
insights.locator: Thailand: managing surplus capacity
